newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A -- Part IV, No tool to prick bubble.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A -- Part IV, No tool to prick bubble.

text.p: Following are excerpts from the question and answer session of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan before the House Banking Monetary Policy subcommittee on Wednesday.
Greenspan delivered the second and final leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins address at 1400 EST/1900 GMT.

Rep. LEACH: " ... As I'm sitting here thinking of the problems of wage stagnation ... I'm wondering as Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board would you care to comment on what I consider to be an ethical umbrage of corporate governments ... not only do we have wage stagnation of certain levels but we have incredible compensation escalation at other levels ... describes to be a problem in our system, and I'm wondering ... is this an issue that you would wish to jawbone on?"

GREENSPAN: "No, but I must say that when I was in the private sector, when I actually had some capabilities on a number of boards, I argued that stock options should not be priced directly, but priced as a ratio to the overall stock-price level ... if one is doing something in corporate governance, which is competitively superior to everyone else, one should be rewarded; but one should not be rewarded if the stock market overall goes up, which drags up all prices irrespective if a company is doing well or not well. I would suggest to you that if that type of a view had prevailed, which it clearly has not ... many of these outside compensation packages that you're looking at would not at this stage exist."
LEACH: " ... Would you care to comment and perhaps with the historical perspective ... of the rational for commenting on the market itself, how appropriate or inappropriate is that?"

GREENSPAN: "As economies become more complex internationalized, and as balance sheets -- both household and corporate -- had increasingly become factors in the economic outlook in the production of goods and services, we have had to broaden our view of the particular range of issues which we cover in the context of developing monetary policy. It's probably inevitable as standards of living overall rise, the assets that individuals have become an increasing part of their decisions to spend or not spend.

Therefore, because of the fact that of necessity, and because of a lag monetary policy invariably has with respect of the economy, we have to forecast what we think is developing in the economy. Were we not to be looking at balance sheets and asset spillovers ... I don't think we would be getting a full comprehensive understanding what the forces driving the economy are. I decided that we can not be making changes up or down in the federal funds rate ... we cannot be making changes up or down in the federal funds rate without a fairly extensive explanation to the Congress and the American people of what the factors are we are looking at.

"Years ago, we looked mainly at money supply and a fairly restricted range and we communicated that as best we could and as a consequence of that it was pretty easy to communicate why we were moving policy one way or another since money supply has grown in a matter of recent years which has been inconsistent with economic events and only recently has seemed to get closer to normal. We have been forced to broaden the whole area of evolving forces to make judgments as to how the economy functions.

We, therefore, concluded that it was necessary for us to express the fact that we were doing that, and to evaluate the various changes in balance sheets and markets in much the same way we do in home building, personal-consumption expenditures, consumer debt and export markets.

"I recognize as soon as we raised the issue in my speech last December about the nature of the stock market that it would probably have some effect. However, I did not speculate as to which direction I thought the market was going, I was really raising a broad question.

Today, in my prepared remarks ... I take a look at the various factors affecting the stock market and conclude that if profit margins continue to rise, as analysts on Wall Street expect them to, then the market is properly priced as best as we can judge on the basis of the level of where interest rates are. If, however, profit margins, which are quite high, but below where they were in the 1960s, don't go any further, then the market will run into some difficulty. I think in the process of evaluating that, we don't know what is likely to happen ...

"Is it possible for margins to rise further? It certainly is. At this rate of inflation, back in the 1960s, margins were indeed higher from where they are now, so that the spike they've come up considerable way since 1991, they could very well continue further as analysts expect them to.

"Our basic judgement is that we need to look at all of these various things and we have to communicate our views to the Congress if we're going to give you an essential view of the types of things we are going to look at. The one thing I was not endeavoring to do, because I don't think it is possible to do, is to jawbone the stock market.

"Stock markets in this world, especially in the United States, are extremely sophisticated, complex, very liquid institutions, with millions of investors. You cannot talk those markets up or down; anyone who thinks they can has just not looked at the evidence. What we will inevitably be required to do as the years go on, and as this economy becomes increasingly more complex, and especially as an ever increasing proportion of American households own all sorts of assets, we are going to have to evaluate how they will respond to price changes

... and what I was endeavoring to do and to effectively try to communicate today and to your Senate colleagues last week, is what has evolved as a natural consequence of the increased complexity of the economic system with which we are dealing. It is not any longer ... a simple thing (with) which to deal. We use a number of different techniques for evaluating what are fundamental processes; we believe that our goal is maximum sustainable economic growth, but that in our judgment requires low inflation or more appropriately stable prices.

"Our evaluation of that process, whether we look at the supply and demand forces which are driving the economy or direct measures of inflationary expectations, such as the gold price or money supply -- if it ever gets back into place -- and the newly issued indexed bonds; these are all elements involved in how we endeavored to determine what is going on as best we can and to make a judgment as to what as a consequence is the most appropriate policy stance. So it is not a stock market issue we are involved with ... we don't view monetary policy as a tool to prick the stock market bubble ... What we do is look at a wide variety of things -- income and consumption, assets and liabilities -- combining them all to make judgments as to what it is that one should be doing with respect to our policy stance."
